title: Build procedural fluency from conceptual understanding
subtitle: Understanding first, then fluency — so procedures are flexible tools students can reconstruct, not fragile steps they memorized and forget.

sections.sources: Source: NCTM, Principles to Actions (2014) · Adding It Up (2001).

blocks.text: Effective teaching builds fluency with procedures on a foundation of conceptual understanding, so that over time students become skillful in using procedures flexibly as they solve problems.

The order matters. When the concept comes first, the procedure has something to hold onto — students can reconstruct it, catch their own errors, and know when to use it. When the procedure comes first (“just cross-multiply,” “just flip and multiply”), it sits on nothing and washes out by the next unit. Fluency is the *goal*; understanding is the *foundation*. This is the practice that most directly refutes “drill it until it sticks.”
What it looks like in grades 6–8

items: Students develop a strategy from reasoning, then practice it to fluency — in that order.
Fluency defined as **flexible, accurate, efficient, and appropriate**, not just fast.
Practice that still asks for reasoning: “which method is most efficient here, and why?”
Standard algorithms introduced as the efficient version of something students already understand.

yes.title: We want to see & hear
items: “Why does that procedure work?” answered by students
Practice that follows understanding, not replaces it
Self-correction because the concept is there to check against

no.title: We should *not* see
items: Tricks with no meaning (butterfly, keep-change-flip as the whole lesson)
Fluency practice before any understanding is built

blocks.text: Where it lives in our toolbelt

This is the whole logic of our opener routines — [Number Talks & Strings](/math/approach/number-talks) build rational-number fluency *from* reasoning. It then governs [Fluency Practice](/math/approach/fluency-practice), where monitoring keeps practice connected to meaning, and it’s the reason our [Spiral Review](/math/approach/spiral-review) asks for strategy, not just recall.
Before teaching a procedure, ask: “what’s the idea that makes this work?” Teach that first. The steps then become something students can rebuild — not something they have to remember cold.
